# Plan: Multi-tenant Auth Refactor (reviewed)

## Implementation Tasks
Synthesized from this review's findings. Each task derives from a specific
finding above. Run with Claude Code or Codex; checkbox as you ship.

- [ ] **T1 (P1, human: ~3h / CC: ~10min)** — auth/router — Add `routeAuth()` with `AUTH_V2_ENABLED` kill switch and `AUTH_V2_TENANTS` allowlist; `legacyAuthFlow()` unchanged
  - Surfaced by: Scope Challenge S4 / Architecture A3 (D4, D9)
  - Files: `auth/router.ts`, `auth/router.test.ts`
  - Verify: 4 routing branch tests green
- [ ] **T2 (P1, human: ~4h / CC: ~15min)** — auth/AuthCache — Create facade over the existing adapter with `Reader` (`get`, `invalidate`) and `Writer` (`set`) interfaces; no module-level export
  - Surfaced by: Architecture A1, A2 (D6, D7, D8)
  - Files: `auth/AuthCache.ts`, `auth/AuthCache.test.ts`
  - Verify: isolation + key + writer-only tests green; adapter tests untouched and green
- [ ] **T3 (P1, human: ~1d / CC: ~30min)** — auth/AuthBroker — Implement with injected `Writer`; `validate()` returns `AuthResult`; `Promise.all` over 5 IDP calls with shared `AbortController` and 3 s deadline; composition root wires one cache
  - Surfaced by: Architecture A1/A4, Code quality C1, Performance P1/P2 (D7, D10, D13, D14)
  - Files: `auth/AuthBroker.ts`, `auth/AuthBroker.test.ts`, `auth/composition.ts`
  - Verify: hit=0 calls; one-rejects; deadline; sibling-abort; elapsed≈max tests green
- [ ] **T4 (P1, human: ~4h / CC: ~15min)** — auth/SessionMint — Implement with injected `Reader` only; return minted session to `AuthBroker` for storage
  - Surfaced by: Architecture A2 (D8)
  - Files: `auth/SessionMint.ts`, `auth/SessionMint.test.ts`
  - Verify: type test (no `set`); late-mint-does-not-repopulate test green
- [ ] **T5 (P1, human: ~1d / CC: ~20min)** — auth/validateAndDispatch — Split into `validate()` + `dispatch()`; map known errors to `AuthResult`; rethrow unknown; header diagram
  - Surfaced by: Code quality C1 (D10)
  - Files: `auth/validateAndDispatch.ts`, `auth/validateAndDispatch.test.ts`
  - Verify: one test per variant + unknown-propagates + no-dispatch-on-non-ok green
- [ ] **T6 (P1, human: ~1.5d / CC: ~30min)** — tests/parity — Write `authBehavior.contract.test.ts` parameterized over `legacyAuthFlow()` and `AuthBroker`
  - Surfaced by: Test review T1 CRITICAL (D11)
  - Files: `auth/authBehavior.contract.test.ts` (or `tests/`)
  - Verify: six scenarios green for both implementations before any tenant is allowlisted
- [ ] **T7 (P2, human: ~1d / CC: ~30min)** — tests/e2e — Write `auth.e2e.test.ts`: legacy login, v2 login, tenant suspension denial, kill-switch rollback mid-session
  - Surfaced by: Test review T2 (D12)
  - Files: `auth/auth.e2e.test.ts`
  - Verify: 4 flows green against IDP stub in CI
- [ ] **T8 (P2, human: ~1h / CC: ~5min)** — docs — Header ASCII diagrams in `AuthBroker.ts`, `validateAndDispatch.ts`, `router.ts`
  - Surfaced by: Architecture A5, Code quality C4
  - Files: `auth/AuthBroker.ts`, `auth/validateAndDispatch.ts`, `auth/router.ts`
  - Verify: diagrams match the routing table and variant map
- [ ] **T9 (P3, human: ~30min / CC: ~5min)** — TODOS.md — Create with the four approved entries below
  - Surfaced by: Final planning decisions D15-D18
  - Files: `TODOS.md`
  - Verify: file matches TODOS-format (What/Why/Context/Effort/Priority)

Effort assumption: tests ~50x, features ~30x, architecture ~5x human÷CC ratios, adjusted down for a 3-component auth change.

JSONL artifact: `~/.gstack/projects/gstack-plan-count-Sr94jU/tasks-eng-review-20260915-192142.jsonl` (9 tasks).

## Worktree parallelization strategy

| Step | Modules touched | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| T5 `AuthResult` type + `validate/dispatch` split | auth/ (validateAndDispatch) | — |
| T2 `AuthCache` facade | auth/ (AuthCache) | — |
| T3 `AuthBroker` + composition root | auth/ | T2, T5 |
| T4 `SessionMint` | auth/ | T2 |
| T1 router + flags | auth/ (router) | T3 |
| T6 parity suite | auth/__tests__ or tests/ | legacy only at first; T3 to parameterize |
| T7 E2E | tests/e2e | T1, T3, T4 |
| T8 diagrams | auth/ headers | T1, T3, T5 |
| T9 TODOS.md | repo root | after plan mode exits |

Lanes:
- Lane A: T5 → T2 → T3 + T4 → T1 → T8 (sequential, shared `auth/`)
- Lane B: T6 parity suite written against `legacyAuthFlow()` (independent: tests/ only), then parameterized over `AuthBroker` after Lane A's T3 merges
- Lane C: T7 E2E (after A and B merge)
- T9 anywhere (root only)

Execution: launch A and B in parallel worktrees. Merge both. Then C.
Conflict flag: if the parity suite is placed under `auth/` instead of `tests/`, Lanes A and B both touch `auth/`; keep it under `tests/` or `auth/__tests__/` to avoid the merge conflict.

questions.question:
D4 — Keep the legacyAuthFlow() rewrite in this PR, or strangle it?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor; Scope Challenge feature cut #1 of 2.
ELI10: The plan rewrites the existing `legacyAuthFlow()` in the same change that adds AuthBroker and SessionMint (PLAN.md:27-28), and the planned tests deliberately skip it (PLAN.md:14-16). That means the one code path every current user logs in through gets replaced with zero proof it still behaves the same. A strangler approach lands the new services first, routes traffic to them behind a flag, and rewrites the legacy path as its own step once a regression suite exists.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a rewrite-in-place with no net means a login regression shows up in production for every tenant at once, with no flag to flip back. Deferring too long means two auth paths live side by side for a while.
Recommendation: B because it makes the change reversible (flag flip) and separates structural change from behavioral change (Beck); the regression suite this review will require lands before the rewrite, not after. (human: ~2 days / CC: ~30 min for the flag + routing.)
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score. Whichever you choose, regression coverage for legacyAuthFlow() is still required and is decided separately in the Test review.
Net: one big-bang swap vs. two smaller reversible steps.

options.label: Defer rewrite: strangler behind a flag (recommended)
options.description:
✅ New services ship with a rollback switch; legacy path stays live until proven replaceable
✅ Regression suite is written against the running legacy code, then the rewrite has a target to hit
❌ Two auth paths coexist for one release; flag and routing code must be removed later

options.label: Include: rewrite legacyAuthFlow() in this PR
options.description:
✅ One PR, one review, no temporary dual-path code to clean up
✅ Callers move to the new services immediately, no flag plumbing
❌ No rollback short of revert; regression tests must be written from the old code before it is deleted

options.label: Cut: do not touch legacyAuthFlow() at all
options.description:
✅ Smallest possible diff; zero risk to the current login path
✅ New services can still be built and tested in isolation
❌ Refactor goal is not met; legacy path never converges on the new architecture

answers.D4 \u2014 Keep the legacyAuthFlow() rewr: Defer rewrite: strangler behind a flag (recommended)

questions.question:
D6 — Component arrangement: keep TokenStore as a separate class, or fold it into AuthCache?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor; Scope Challenge structure choice (feature choices held fixed: legacy rewrite deferred behind a flag per D4, RequestPolicy deferred per D5).
ELI10: With RequestPolicy deferred, the plan still adds four components: AuthBroker, SessionMint, AuthCache, and TokenStore. The plan says AuthCache is a facade over the existing cache adapter, which already stores tokens keyed by tenant/issuer/audience/policy and already handles eviction and invalidation (PLAN.md:7-13). That makes TokenStore a third layer doing the adapter's job. This question picks structure only: how many boxes. Whether the shared AuthCache stays a module-level global (Section 1) and how errors and IDP calls are handled are separate decisions and stay pending in every option.
Stakes if we pick wrong: too many layers means three places to look when a tenant's revoked token still validates at 3am; too few means AuthBroker and SessionMint tangle if their responsibilities really are distinct.
Recommendation: A because it removes the one component whose job the existing adapter already does, keeps the two services whose names describe distinct work, and preserves every retained contract from PLAN.md:6-13 unchanged. (human: ~0.5 day less / CC: ~5 min less.)
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: the existing adapter is already the token store; the question is whether you want a second one.

options.description:
✅ AuthCache facade + existing adapter is the single token store; one place for invalidation bugs
✅ Two services with distinct names keep brokering and minting separable and testable
❌ If TokenStore was meant to hold something the adapter cannot (e.g. refresh-token secrets), that need has to be named and added to AuthCache

options.label: 4 components: keep TokenStore separate (original)
options.description:
✅ Matches the plan as written; no re-scoping of what AuthCache owns
✅ Room for TokenStore to own a distinct persistence concern if one exists
❌ Three storage layers (adapter, AuthCache, TokenStore) with no stated boundary between the last two

✅ Simplest wiring for the D4 flag routing

questions.question:
D7 — How should AuthBroker and SessionMint get their AuthCache: injected instance or module-level global?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor; Architecture finding A1 (PLAN.md:19-20), ledger row R1.
ELI10: Right now the plan has both new services `import` one shared AuthCache object that lives at the top of a module. That works until a test wants a fresh cache, two copies of the package get installed, or someone needs to know who else is touching the cache. Injecting the one instance through each service's constructor from a single composition root keeps exactly one backing cache (the contract at PLAN.md:12 stays) but makes the dependency visible and swappable. Concurrent-write safety (R2) and flag granularity (R3) stay pending in both options.
Stakes if we pick wrong: with the global, a test that pollutes the cache silently affects the next test file, and a production bug where tenant A's entry appears in tenant B's request has no obvious owner to trace.
Recommendation: A because it is the standard fix [Layer 1], costs one constructor parameter per service, and makes the R2 safety work testable with a fake cache. (human: ~2h / CC: ~5 min.)
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: one extra constructor argument vs. hidden shared state in the auth path.

options.label: Inject one AuthCache instance via constructors (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Tests construct a fresh cache per case; no cross-file leakage under Vitest/Jest workers
✅ Dependency is explicit at the call site; composition root is the one place the cache is created
❌ Every place that instantiates AuthBroker or SessionMint must pass the cache (one composition root plus tests)

options.label: Keep the module-level export (as planned)
options.description:
✅ Zero wiring changes; services import and go
✅ Matches the plan text exactly, no re-plan
❌ Test isolation depends on module-cache resets; two writers on an invisible global is the exact pattern that produced A2

answers.D7 \u2014 How should AuthBroker and Sess: Inject one AuthCache instance via constructors (recommended)

questions.question:
D8 — How do two services write to one AuthCache without a revoked token coming back to life?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor; Architecture finding A2 (PLAN.md:10 + :20), ledger row R2.
ELI10: The plan says the adapter does not serialize mutations and that both new services mutate the cache. Picture it: an admin suspends a tenant, the invalidation hook clears that tenant's entries, and a millisecond later SessionMint finishes an in-flight mint and writes the entry back. The suspended tenant's token now validates until it expires. This is the classic lost-invalidation race. Two fixes: only one service ever writes (the other asks it to), or every write proves it saw the latest invalidation (a generation counter in the facade, rejected if stale). The adapter and its hooks stay untouched in every option.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a security bug (suspended or revoked tenant still authenticates) that only reproduces under concurrency and never in a unit test.
Recommendation: A because it is explicit over clever: one writer means the race cannot occur by construction, no counters to reason about, and the failure mode is visible in the type signature (SessionMint has no `set`). Option B is correct but adds a concurrency primitive that a tired human at 3am has to understand. (A: human ~4h / CC ~15 min. B: human ~1 day / CC ~30 min.)
Completeness: A=10/10, B=10/10, C=3/10
Net: eliminate the race structurally vs. detect it per write vs. leave it in.

options.label: Single writer: only AuthBroker writes to AuthCache (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Lost-invalidation race is impossible by construction; nothing to reason about under load
✅ SessionMint's API cannot mutate the cache, so the guarantee is visible in the types and enforced at compile time
❌ SessionMint must hand minted sessions to AuthBroker for storage, one extra call and one extra unit test seam

options.label: Generation-checked writes: set(key, value, gen) rejects stale gens
options.description:
✅ Both services keep write access; race is detected and the stale write dropped
✅ Generalizes if a third writer ever appears
❌ A per-key generation counter in the facade is new concurrency machinery in the auth path; harder to test and debug than no shared writes

options.label: Do nothing: two unordered writers (as planned)
options.description:
✅ No change to the plan; smallest diff
✅ Adapter behavior identical to today
❌ Revoked or suspended tenant tokens can be re-cached by a late write; no test can reliably catch it

answers.D8 \u2014 How do two services write to o: Single writer: only AuthBroker writes to AuthCache (recommended)

questions.question:
D9 — What shape is the strangler flag: per-tenant allowlist with a kill switch, or one global boolean?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor; Architecture finding A3, ledger row R3 (D4 approved "a flag", shape undecided).
ELI10: D4 put the new AuthBroker/SessionMint path behind a flag with legacyAuthFlow() still live. The flag can be one switch for everyone, or a list of tenant IDs that get the new path plus a global off switch. This is a multi-tenant system: a per-tenant list lets you turn on one internal tenant, watch it, then widen. A global boolean is all-or-nothing.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a global flip that goes wrong logs out every tenant at once; a per-tenant list is a few more lines of config parsing and one more test.
Recommendation: A because reversibility and canaries are the whole point of the strangler (D4), and the tenant ID is already on every request path per the cache key contract (PLAN.md:7). (A: human ~3h / CC ~10 min. B: human ~1h / CC ~5 min.)
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10
Net: canary by tenant vs. one big switch.

options.label: Per-tenant allowlist + global kill switch (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Roll out to one internal tenant first; widen tenant by tenant with the legacy path untouched for the rest
✅ Kill switch overrides the list, so rollback is one env var regardless of how many tenants are enabled
❌ Two config values to document and parse; one more routing test (tenant in list, not in list, kill switch on)

options.label: Single global boolean
options.description:
✅ Simplest routing: one `if`, one env var, one test
✅ Good enough if there is exactly one tenant in the first environment you enable it in
❌ Turning it on is a fleet-wide switch; a bug affects every tenant at once, which is what D4 was trying to avoid

questions.question:
D10 — Rewrite validateAndDispatch() with explicit error outcomes, or just add logging to the three catches?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor; Code quality finding C1 (PLAN.md:23-24), ledger row R4.
ELI10: Today three nested try/catch blocks each quietly eat one kind of error. An expired token, a revoked one, and an unreachable identity provider all vanish into the same silence, and whatever runs after the catches may proceed as if nothing happened. The fix is to split the function: `validate()` returns a typed result (ok / expired / revoked / idp_unreachable) and rethrows anything it does not recognize, then `dispatch()` branches on that result. The user gets a specific failure, and an unknown bug crashes loudly instead of being swallowed.
Stakes if we pick wrong: with swallowed errors, an IDP outage can look like "everyone's token is invalid" (or worse, dispatch runs on an unvalidated request) and nobody finds out until a tenant complains.
Recommendation: A because it is explicit over clever, kills the error-hiding anti-pattern at the root, and each outcome gets its own test. The plan's own 5-call IDP path (Section 4) needs the idp_unreachable variant anyway. (A: human ~1 day / CC ~20 min. B: human ~1h / CC ~5 min.)
Completeness: A=10/10, B=5/10, C=1/10
Net: typed outcomes and loud unknowns vs. the same silence with log lines.

options.label: Split into validate() + dispatch() with a typed AuthResult (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Every known error class becomes a visible outcome the caller and the user can act on
✅ Unknown errors propagate, so a real bug surfaces in monitoring instead of being eaten
❌ Touches every caller of validateAndDispatch() to branch on the result (bounded: it is one function)

options.label: Keep the nesting, add a log line per catch
options.description:
✅ Smallest diff; the swallowed errors at least show up in logs
✅ No caller changes
❌ Behavior still silently continues after failure; three nested blocks remain the next person's problem

options.label: Do nothing (as planned)
options.description:
✅ Zero effort now
✅ No risk of changing current caller behavior
❌ Error hiding stays in the auth path; failures are invisible to users and operators

answers.D10 \u2014 Rewrite validateAndDispatch(): Split into validate() + dispatch() with a typed AuthResult (recommended)

questions.question:
D11 — How do we cover legacyAuthFlow() against regression: a shared parity suite, a characterization suite, or a router pass-through test?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor; Test review finding T1 CRITICAL (PLAN.md:14-16, :27-28), ledger row R5.
ELI10: The plan says the new tests will not touch legacyAuthFlow() at all. After D4 it is untouched code, but every current login now reaches it through a new router, and the whole point of the strangler is to later replace it with AuthBroker. A parity suite is one set of scenario tests (valid token, expired, revoked, tenant suspended, IDP down) run against BOTH implementations: it pins today's behavior now and becomes the acceptance test for the rewrite later. A characterization suite pins legacy only. A pass-through test only proves the router forwards calls.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a login regression for every tenant with nothing that would have caught it; or a rewrite later with no target to hit.
Recommendation: A because it is the complete version and costs almost nothing extra with CC: the same five scenarios must be written for AuthBroker anyway, so running them against legacy too is a fixture parameter, not a second suite. (A: human ~1.5 days / CC ~30 min. B: human ~1 day / CC ~20 min. C: human ~1h / CC ~5 min.)
Completeness: A=10/10, B=8/10, C=4/10
Net: one suite that guards today and specifies tomorrow vs. a snapshot of today vs. proof the router forwards.

options.label: Shared parity suite run against legacy AND AuthBroker (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Pins current legacy behavior and doubles as the acceptance test for the deferred rewrite
✅ Divergence between the two paths shows up as a red test before any tenant is switched over
❌ Scenarios must be written as implementation-agnostic fixtures (inputs, expected outcome, expected cache key)

options.label: Characterization suite for legacyAuthFlow() only
options.description:
✅ Pins today's outcomes and cache writes for every scenario
✅ No coupling to AuthBroker's test shape
❌ Written once for legacy, then rewritten again for the rewrite; parity is never asserted

options.label: Router pass-through test only
options.description:
✅ Minimal: proves the router forwards args and returns the legacy result
✅ Fast to write
❌ Says nothing about what legacyAuthFlow() actually does; the rewrite starts with no net

answers.D11 \u2014 How do we cover legacyAuthFlo: Shared parity suite run against legacy AND AuthBroker (recommended)

questions.question:
D12 — Add four end-to-end tests for the flagged auth flows, or stop at unit + integration?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor; Test review finding T2, ledger row R7. Unit/integration tests for D7-D11 are already approved work; this only decides E2E depth.
ELI10: Unit tests prove each piece works with fakes. The four flows here span router → service → cache → adapter → IDP, and auth is the one place where mocks hiding a real wiring mistake costs the most. The four E2E cases: a tenant off the list logs in (legacy), a tenant on the list logs in (AuthBroker), an admin suspends a tenant and the next request is denied, and the kill switch is flipped while sessions are live and legacy takes over cleanly.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a wiring bug (wrong cache injected, router reads the wrong env var) passes every unit test and fails in the first environment you enable it in.
Recommendation: A because the E2E decision matrix names auth flows as too important for unit tests alone, and the strangler rollout depends on the kill-switch flow working the first time it is needed. (A: human ~1 day / CC ~30 min. B: no extra work.)
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10
Net: proof the assembled system routes and rolls back vs. proof each part works alone.

options.label: Add the 4 E2E flows (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Catches composition-root and env-var wiring mistakes that fakes cannot see
✅ Kill-switch rollback is rehearsed in CI before it is ever needed in production
❌ Needs an IDP stub or sandbox reachable from CI; slower than the unit suite

options.label: Unit + integration only
options.description:
✅ No E2E infrastructure to stand up; faster CI
✅ Parity suite (D11) and per-branch router tests still cover the logic
❌ Wiring across router/service/cache/adapter is never exercised as one system before rollout

questions.question:
D13 — Parallelize the 5 IDP calls with Promise.all?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor; Performance finding P1 (PLAN.md:31-32), ledger row R6. Timeout and cancellation are a separate row (R8) and stay pending here.
ELI10: On every cache miss, token validation asks the identity provider five questions one after another. The plan says the five are independent, so they can be asked at the same time and the wait drops from the sum of five round trips to the slowest single one. Because auth needs all five answers, `Promise.all` (fail if any fails) is the right aggregator, not `allSettled`; a failure maps to the `idp_unreachable` outcome approved in D10.
Stakes if we pick wrong: leaving it sequential means every first login per tenant per policy version pays ~5x latency; parallelizing without verifying independence would be the real risk, but the plan states they are independent (verify during implementation).
Recommendation: A because the plan itself calls it trivial, the calls are stated independent, and the win is a straight ~5x on cold-cache logins. (A: human ~2h / CC ~10 min.)
Completeness: A=10/10, B=3/10
Net: one slow round trip vs. five in a row.

options.label: Promise.all over the 5 calls (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Cache-miss latency drops from the sum of five calls to the slowest one
✅ Any single failure fails validation, which is the correct semantics for auth; maps to idp_unreachable
❌ Five concurrent connections per miss instead of one at a time; stampede mitigation is a separate TODO

options.label: Keep the calls sequential
options.description:
✅ No change; lowest concurrent load on the IDP
✅ Early exit on first failure without extra cancellation logic
❌ Every cold-cache login waits ~5x longer than it needs to

questions.question:
D14 — Put a deadline on IDP validation, and cancel the sibling calls when one fails?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor; Performance finding P2 / Architecture A4, ledger row R8 (R6 Promise.all approved in D13 and held fixed).
ELI10: Nothing in the plan says how long a login may wait on the identity provider. With five parallel calls, when one fails `Promise.all` reports failure right away, but the other four keep running and holding connections. During an IDP brownout that turns into piles of open sockets and logins that hang until the OS gives up. The fix is one shared `AbortController` per validation: a deadline (3 seconds, configurable) and an abort of the remaining calls as soon as one fails or the deadline hits. The result maps to the `idp_unreachable` outcome from D10.
Stakes if we pick wrong: an IDP slowdown becomes a login outage for every tenant, with connection exhaustion spreading to unrelated requests on the same process.
Recommendation: A because it is stdlib (`AbortController` + `AbortSignal.timeout`) [Layer 1], a few lines, and the only option that bounds both wall time and resource use. 3 s is a starting default; tune it to the IDP's p99. (A: human ~3h / CC ~10 min. B: human ~1h / CC ~5 min.)
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10, C=1/10
Net: bounded wait and bounded sockets vs. bounded wait only vs. hope the IDP is fast.

options.label: Deadline 3 s + abort siblings on first failure (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Login never waits longer than the deadline; user gets idp_unreachable instead of a spinner
✅ Failed validations release their four sibling connections immediately, so brownouts do not pile up sockets
❌ One more env var (AUTH_IDP_TIMEOUT_MS) to document; the IDP client must accept an AbortSignal

options.label: Deadline only, no sibling cancellation
options.description:
✅ Bounds user-visible wait with less plumbing
✅ No dependency on the IDP client honoring AbortSignal
❌ Sibling calls keep running to completion after a failure; socket pile-up under brownout remains

options.label: No timeout (as planned)
options.description:
✅ Zero work
✅ Relies on the HTTP client's default socket timeout, if any
❌ Login hang duration is undefined; IDP slowness becomes a full auth outage

answers.D14 \u2014 Put a deadline on IDP validat: Deadline 3 s + abort siblings on first failure (recommended)

D17 — TODO 3 of 4: capture the pre-existing hook-vs-in-flight-write race in the cache adapter?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor; surfaced as a factual correction under D8.
ELI10: D8 made AuthBroker the only service that writes to the cache, which kills the race between the two new services. A second, older race remains inside the unchanged adapter: an invalidation hook (logout, revocation, suspension) can fire between a validation finishing and its cache write landing, so the freshly-invalidated entry gets written back and lives until expiry. This exists today with the current code and is out of this PR's scope (the adapter is retained unchanged per PLAN.md:12-13).
What: Make cache writes invalidation-aware in the adapter or facade (e.g. per-tenant invalidation generation checked on set, or re-check tenant/revocation state immediately before write).
Why: A suspended or revoked tenant can authenticate until token expiry if the timing lines up; the window is small but the impact is a security bypass.
Pros: closes the last resurrection path; the D11 parity suite gives a place to add the concurrency test.
Cons: touches the adapter this plan promised not to touch; needs a real concurrency test harness.
Context: Race window = time between last IDP response and AuthCache.set(). Reproduce with a fake adapter that fires invalidate() during that window. Start in the AuthCache facade (D6/D7) since it fronts every write.
Depends on: this PR shipped (AuthCache facade exists).
Effort: M. Priority: P1.
Stakes if we pick wrong: an unrecorded security race in the auth path.
Recommendation: A because it is a security-relevant gap with a concrete reproduction path, and building it now would break the "adapter unchanged" contract this review held fixed.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: a recorded P1 with a repro vs. an unrecorded race.

options.label: Add to TODOS.md (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Security-relevant race gets a P1 entry with the repro recipe and the file to start in
✅ Adapter contract for this PR stays intact
❌ The window stays open until the follow-up lands

options.label: Skip — not valuable enough
options.description:
✅ No new tracked work
✅ Window is small in practice
❌ Known security race with no record; next reader rediscovers it from scratch

options.label: Build it now in this PR

✅ Concurrency test lands with the parity suite

questions.question:
D18 — TODO 4 of 4: capture cold-cache stampede protection (in-flight dedupe) for AuthBroker?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor; Performance finding P3 (medium confidence 6/10).
ELI10: With D13, every cache miss fires five IDP calls at once. After a deploy, or when the kill switch flips back on, the cache is cold and every request for the same tenant/token misses at the same moment. N concurrent misses become 5N IDP calls for the same answer. A singleflight map (one in-flight validation promise per cache key; later callers await it) turns that into 5 calls total. This is an optimization beyond the plan and its need depends on IDP rate limits this review could not see.
What: In AuthBroker.validate(), keep a Map<cacheKey, Promise<AuthResult>> of in-flight validations; concurrent misses for the same key await the first.
Why: Prevents a 5x call burst to the IDP on cold cache; protects against IDP rate-limit rejections turning into idp_unreachable for real users.
Pros: small, self-contained; no new dependency; measurable in the fake-IDP test (call count).
Cons: speculative until IDP rate limits are known; adds a Map to reason about (must delete entry on settle).
Context: Only matters if IDP concurrency limits are tighter than peak login rate x 5. Check the IDP's documented limits first; if generous, close this as not needed.
Depends on: D13 shipped; IDP rate-limit numbers.
Effort: S. Priority: P3.
Stakes if we pick wrong: either a stampede at the first cold start or a few lines nobody needed.
Recommendation: A because the check (read the IDP limits) is cheap and the fix is small; recording it beats rediscovering it during an incident.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: a P3 with a go/no-go check vs. finding out at the first cold start.

options.label: Add to TODOS.md (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Stampede risk is recorded with the one fact needed to decide it (IDP rate limits)
✅ Fix is a few lines when and if it is needed
❌ May be closed as unnecessary; minor TODO noise

options.label: Skip — not valuable enough
options.description:
✅ Nothing speculative in the backlog
✅ IDP may well tolerate the burst
❌ First cold start after enabling v2 is the moment you find out

options.label: Build it now in this PR
options.description:
✅ Ships with the parallelization it protects against
✅ Fake-IDP test can assert call count under concurrent misses
❌ Adds concurrency state to AuthBroker before knowing it is needed; widens the PR

D12 — R6: Cache per-issuer IDP metadata (discovery doc, JWKS, tenant config) so most validations skip the network entirely?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor; Performance review, R5 approved (parallel calls with idpCall wrapper).
ELI10: Parallelizing (R5) turns 5 round trips into 1 round trip of latency, but every cache miss still makes 5 network calls. If some of those 5 fetch things that rarely change for a given IDP issuer (its discovery document, its signing keys, a tenant's config), those responses can be cached per issuer with a TTL and most validations would make 0 or 1 calls. I do not know what the 5 calls are; the plan does not list them. R5 already includes a task to enumerate them. Deciding on caching before that list exists would be guessing.
Stakes if we pick wrong: build a metadata cache for calls that turn out to be all per-token (introspection, userinfo) and it is dead code; skip it when 3 of the 5 are static metadata and you leave a 60-80% network reduction on the table plus an IDP hammering risk at scale.
Recommendation: C because the R5 enumeration produces exactly the information this decision needs, at no extra cost; choose with facts, not guesses. This is an outside-style policy row: keep other approved choices fixed.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: decide now blind vs decide right after a task you are already doing.

options.label: C) Investigate before choosing (recommended)
options.description:
✅ The R5 call enumeration (already accepted) tells you which calls are static metadata; this row is re-asked with that list in hand (human: ~1h / CC: ~5 min)
✅ No dead code and no missed win; the decision waits exactly as long as it needs to
❌ Leaves one pending row in the ledger; the plan reports it as an unresolved decision until the enumeration is done

options.label: A) Apply: add per-issuer metadata cache now
options.description:
✅ If the calls include discovery/JWKS/tenant config, cache misses drop to 0-1 network calls and IDP load falls sharply
✅ JWKS refresh-on-unknown-kid is a well-known Layer 1 pattern with little risk
❌ Built before knowing if any of the 5 calls qualify; could be dead code (human: ~1 day / CC: ~30 min)

options.label: B) Keep current value: no metadata cache
options.description:
✅ Nothing to build; R5 already delivers the latency win
✅ No second cache with its own TTL semantics next to the token cache
❌ Every cache miss still makes all 5 network calls; at scale the IDP sees the full validation volume

options.label: D) Defer this proposed change only
options.description:
✅ Removes it from this PR cleanly; can be a TODO with the R5 call list attached
✅ Keeps the PR focused on correctness fixes
❌ Same downside as B for this release, and the decision still has to be made later without the review context
